title: Electrocatalytic Reduction of Carbon Dioxide using Sol-gel Processed Copper Indium Sulfide (CIS) Immobilized on ITO-Coated Glass Electrode
abstract: Sol-gel processed copper indium sulfide (CIS) films have been processed on glass and transparent indium doped tin oxide (ITO)-coated glass electrodes by a straightforward layer by layer spin coating route yielding excellent film qualities with subsequent thermal annealing. Resulting films were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and UV-vis spectroscopy. We apply these films in an electrochemical cell as a working electrode and take a view on the reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2) to its energy richer carbon monoxide (CO) in acetonitrile solution containing 0.1 M (C4H9)4NPF6 supporting electrolyte saturated with CO2. CIS films exhibit pronounced electrochemical and photoelectrochemical activities. Concomitantly, we quantify the generation of CO, which starts to evolve at a threshold potential of −0.60 V vs normal hydrogen electrode (NHE). The calculated faradaic efficiency of the electrochemical reduction of CO2 into CO exceeds 20 (±1)% in an optimized thin-film structure.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Green plants efficiently capture and convert carbon dioxide (CO2) via photosynthesis into organic molecules which are the building blocks of all living organisms. Most life would not have been evolved without this process [1, 2], demonstrating the importance of CO2 for life. Furthermore, CO2 is also used as a raw material for various industrial processes [3–5].
Though CO2 is such an important gas, it is also considered as one of the greenhouse gases released by both natural and artificial processes [6]. In an ideal case, the CO2 produced on our globe should be counterbalanced with what is consumed, so that its level remains constant to maintain environmental stability. Unfortunately, one of the major challenges of our global society, however, is the rapid increase in the concentration of carbon dioxide due to anthropogenic activities, both by excessive CO2 output into the atmosphere and by reducing the ability of natural sinks, such as forests. The Scripps Institution of Oceanography report in April 2015, displays the current level of atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration estimated to be 401 ppm [7]. Of these emissions, those that are produced from extensive combustion of fossil fuels (coal, natural gas, and oil) for energy, transportation, and industrial processes make the lion share [8].
Regulating the concentration of carbon dioxide is a global challenge. Major attempts undergoing to regulate the concentration of carbon dioxide are carbon dioxide capture [9–11], sequestration [12–16], and utilization/recycling [17–20]. Capture and sequestration in ocean and geological formation is not a long-term solution as it incurs costs and bears risks of leakages [21, 22]. But recycling of CO2 has sustainable potential

tackling two major challenges of our society, i.e., to alleviate looming climate changes and to create storage and transport capabilities for renewable energy [23, 24]. Especially the exploration of sunlight as an effective energy source to reduce carbon dioxide into synthetic fuels (solar fuel) [6, 25–27] and chemical feed stocks could create a sustainable energy source that does not compromise our environment.
Catalytic electrochemical and photoelectrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide into compounds with higher energy content (value added) fuels such as carbon monoxide (CO), formic acid (HCOOH) or formate (HCOO−), oxalic acid (H2C2O4) or oxalate (C2O4
2−), formaldehyde (CH2O), methanol (CH3OH), methane (CH4), ethylene (CH2CH2), ethanol (CH3CH2OH), and others [6, 28–32] has attracted great attention because of controllable electrode potentials, low reaction temperatures, and facile scale-up possibilities. Though the thermodynamic formal reduction potentials vs normal hydrogen electrode (NHE) for carbon dioxide in to such products (−0.7 to −0.2 V vs NHE at pH 7) [6, 27, 30] look feasible, these reactions are kinetically very slow, suffer from high overpotential, and compete with hydrogen formation reaction in protic solvents where CO2 is less soluble [33]. Particularly, the large reorganizational energy required to rearrange the linear CO2 molecule into the bent radical anion (CO2
−) makes a reduction process via a rate limiting initial one-electron transfer highly energy intensive (formal reduction potential −1.9 V vs NHE at pH 7) and difficult to proceed with respect to thermodynamics [19, 34, 35]. In experimental applications, a proper setup of electrodes, catalyst, and supporting electrolyte-solvent composition is required to lower the overpotential or bypass the one-electron transfer mechanism into two electrons and thereby minimizes the competing react ions [36] . In ca ta ly t i c e lec t rochemica l and /o r photoelectrochemical CO2 reduction reactions that use aprotic solvents like acetonitrile, the occurrence of a competing hydrogen reduction reaction or reactions with hydrogen ions is avoided. So the products are usually CO and carbonate ion (CO3
−) [37–39] following the reaction in Eq. 1 [40]. The mechanism may also involve tetrabutylammonium cation of supporting electrolyte act as one-electron mediator to promote the reduction of CO2 [41] and dimerization of the radical anion (CO2 −) with CO2 to form oxalate [42].
2CO2 þ 2e−→ COþ CO32− ð1Þ
Among the ternary chalcopyrite compounds, copper indium sulfide (CIS) has many advantages such as high photovoltaic power conversion efficiency (theoretically up to 28 %) and an optimal band gap (∼1.5 eV). Therefore, CIS is an attractive material in solar cell applications and visible light photocatalytic systems [43, 44]. Thin films of this semiconductor compound have been obtained by many methods such as chemical bath deposition [45, 46], spray pyrolysis [47, 48],
and atomic layer deposition [49, 50]. CIS thin films fabricated by electrochemical co-deposition of Cu–In alloy layers followed by sulfurization have shown an interesting photoelectrochemical reduction of CO2 into methanol in 0.1 M acetate buffer electrolyte solution containing 10 mM pyridine [51, 52]. Moreover, it has been shown that thin films of CIS can also be prepared by the sol-gel route [53]. Within this straightforward technique, large area substrates can be coated readily, dopants can be incorporated easily, and thin films are simply prepared under non-vacuum conditions.
In this work, sol-gel-prepared CIS thin absorber films were deposited on ITO-coated glass electrodes and investigated regarding their applicability as a cathode material for electrochemical and photoelectrochemical reduction of CO2. Structural, optical, electrical, and morphological properties have been investigated. The catalytic activity is tested in aprotic media and shows a pronounced reaction profile as shown by cyclic voltammetry. Furthermore, the evolution of CO probed with gas chromatography (GC) and faradaic efficiencies were found to exceed 20 (±1)%.

sections.heading: Preparation of CIS Films
sections.text: CIS thin films were deposited from an aqueous solution of indium(III) nitrate hydrate [(In(NO3)3 xH2O] (99 % SigmaA ld r i ch ) , coppe r ( I I ) n i t r a t e hemipen t ahyd r a t e [(Cu(NO3)2 2.5H2O)] (98 % Sigma-Aldrich), and thiourea (CH4N2S, 99 % Sigma-Aldrich). Each chemical was dissolved separately in glacial acetic acid and ethanol. The three solutions were mixed to yield a composition with defined molar ratio (In/S/Cu=1/6/1.25). After stirring at room temperature for 30min, a small amount of triethanolamine was added to adjust the pH to 4.3. With further stirring of the solution for 12 h, a yellowish transparent solution was obtained. Glass and ITO-coated glass substrates were cleaned successively via ultra-sonication in acetone, isopropanol, Helmanex® solution, and deionized water. CIS films were obtained on glass and ITO-coated glass substrates by spin coating at 3000 rpm for 15 s. The thickness of the films was varied using sequential (layer by layer) spin coating of the solution. The samples were dried on a hot plate under open air condition for 2 min, at 300 °C. Finally, the films were annealed in a furnace at 420 and 460 °C for 30 min in a nitrogen environment.

sections.heading: Characterization of CIS Films
sections.text:
X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the films were recorded using a Rigaku ultima III diffractometer with monochromatic Cu-Kα radiation (λ=0.154 nm), at 40 kV, 30 mA. The optical absorbance of the films was recorded using a double-beam
UV-vis spectrometer (PerkinElmer 45 UV-vis). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) measurement was carried out on a Zeiss Evo 50 system scanning electron microscope. The thickness of the fabricated films was measured with a profilometer (Bruker Dektak XT).
Electrochemical Investigation
The electrochemical experiments were performed using a JAISSLE potentiostat–galvanostat IMP 88 PC. Cyclic voltammetric reductions of carbon dioxide in dark and under illumination of the working electrode were performed in acetonitrile (ROTH, 99.9 %, ≤10 ppm, H, O) containing 0.1 M tetrabutylammonium hexafluorophosphate ((C4H9)4NPF6) in a three-electrode system using a quartz glass cell. The copper indium sulfide (CIS) films on ITO-coated glass are used as working electrode, a Pt sheet functions as counter electrode, and silver/silver chloride (Ag/AgCl) is set as quasi reference electrode. The Ag/AgCl quasi reference electrode was made by electrochemically depositing silver chloride on silver wire (99.9 %) in 1 M HCl using a standard Ag/AgCl reference electrode. The electrode was first cleaned and roughened by cycling 10 times between 290 and −310 mVat a scan rate of 10 mV s−1. The silver chloride was then deposited by polarizing to −110 mV for 120 s and finally to 90 mV for 600 s [54]. A 20 W halogen spotlight source is used for illumination. The solutions were purged with N2 or CO2 under stirring for 30 min before the actual electrochemical experiment is initiated. Scheme 1 shows a schematic picture of the one-compartment cell for the cyclic voltammetry and potentiostatic electrolysis measurements during N2 or CO2 purging (a) and during closed cyclic voltammetry and electrolysis experiments (b).
Potentiostatic CO2 electrolysis experiments are performed at ambient light in a gastight one-compartment cell. The Ag/ AgCl quasi reference electrode was calibrated using the ferrocene/ferrocenium redox couple (Fc/Fc+) as an internal reference. The half-wave potential (E1/2) for Fc/Fc + was
measured at 410 and 415 mV for the used cyclic voltammetry and potentiostatic experiments, respectively. The formal potential (E1/2 for Fc/Fc
+ vs NHE) was defined at 640 mV [55]. The one-compartment cell contained 40 ml of electrolyte solution and 30 ml of gas phase.
Gas chromatography (GC) analysis was conducted on a Thermo Scientific, Trace GC ULTRA equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD), TG-WAXMS (30 m, 0.32 mm ID, 1-μm film) column and helium as carrier gas at a flow rate of 20 ml min−1 and a temperature of 130 °C.

sections.heading: Structure of CIS
sections.text:
Structural identification of the films was carried out using XRD in the range of 2θ, between 10° and 60°. Figure 1 shows the XRD result of the CIS films. The XRD peaks appeared at 2θ=27.89°, 46.30/46.47°, and 54.78/55.07° which corresponds to the (112), (204)/(220), and the (116)/(312) planes of tetragonal CIS semiconductor, respectively, (JCPDS cart no. 01-082-1702). These results are in good agreement with previously published data [56, 57]. An average crystallite grain size of approximately 10–15 nm has been calculated from the broadening of the diffraction line of the (112) plane at 27.9° using the Scherrer Eq. (2), [58] which is in accordance with former findings [59, 60].

According to this expression, extrapolation of the (αhv)2 value in (αhv)2-hv graphics allows the determination of the optical band gap of the specimens, where hv is the photon energy. The band gap value of CIS film was estimated to be 1.36±0.02 eV based on the plot of (αhν)2 vs hν, as shown in the inset of Fig. 2. The observed band gap corresponds well with reported data [62, 63].
Figure 3 shows SEM images of a CIS film annealed at 420 °C. The surface of the sol-gel derived CIS films depends strongly on the Cu/In molar ratio in the employed solution. As reported in literature, when the Cu/In ratio is below 1.25, the
surface of the film shows many cracks and pin holes [53]. Therefore, in the present work, the Cu/In ratio is fixed to 1.25. As can be seen in the SEM images in Fig. 3, a rather homogenous CIS film without cracks and pinholes was obtained.
Cyclic Voltammetry
Figure 4 shows the cyclic voltammogram of the electrochemical and photoelectrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide in acetonitrile containing 0.1 M (C4H9)4NPF6 saturated with either with N2 or with CO2. Bare ITO electrode in N2 saturated solution does not show any reduction current at the given potential window which indicates that the solvent supporting electrolyte system does not interfere with reductions in this potential range (Fig. 4, curve a). When the solution is saturated
with carbon dioxide, however, a small reduction current is observed with the onset at −1.6 V vs NHE (Fig. 4, curve b).
Bymodifying the ITO electrode with a thin film (400 nm) of CIS, the electrolyte system under N2 saturation still does not show significant reductive current; rather, a capacitive current in the entire window (Fig. 4, curve c) is observed. This can be expected when a semiconducting film of certain thickness is embedded onto the working electrode [64, 65]. With I tð Þ ¼ CdV tð Þdt , one can determine the double-layer capacity C from the cyclic voltammogram shown in Fig. 4a and c using Δ1/2JITO/CIS=0.25 mA cm −2,Δ1/2JITO=7.84 μA cm −2, and v= 20 mV s−1. Then, the specific double-layer capacities of the projected electrode area are estimated to be 0.2 mF cm−2 for pure ITO and 6.3 mF cm−2 for the ITO/CIS electrode. This result suggests an increased surface area of ITO/CIS compared to the bare ITO. When the solution is saturated with CO2 for 30 min, a significant reduction current (−0.59 mA cm−2) is
observed with its onset at −0.60 V vs NHE in dark condition (Fig. 4, curve d). Illumination of the working electrode with white light further increased the reduction current to −0.68 mA cm−2 (Fig. 4, curve e). This photocatalytic effect was also clearly observed in Figure S6 during the light on and off experiment, while the potentiostatic carbon dioxide reduction was undergoing. These high reduction currents in dark and under illumination in contrast to the bare ITO electrode (Fig. 4, curves b, d, and e) show the significant electrochemical and photoelectrochemical catalytic effect of at the CIS-modified ITO electrodes. The reduction product of this electrochemical reaction was confirmed to be carbon monoxide using gas chromatographic analysis. With inert electrodes like Pt, the reduction of CO2 into CO is observed at higher negative potentials around −2.0 V vs NHE [31]. But here, due to the electrocatalytic activity of CIS film, the reduction onset was observed earlier at significantly lower potential (−0.6 V vs NHE).
Table 1 lists the temperature and thickness dependence on electrochemical or photoelectrochemical activity of CIS films coated on ITO. Three different thicknesses in combination with two different annealing temperatures (420 and 460 °C) are used. As can be seen in the table and Figures S1–S5, the maximum currents values recorded at −1.77 V vs NHE from the cyclic voltammograms show that with increasing the thickness, the current density gets reduced and dominated by the capacitive current in the cyclic voltammograms.
Figure 5 shows cyclic voltammograms of CIS-modified ITO electrodes with various film thicknesses (400, 800, and 1000 nm). The film with 400 nm thickness shows the highest reduction current density. A further reduction of this layer thickness increases the probability of finding holes in the final films. So, it looks a thickness of 400 nm is sufficient to catalyze the reaction. Concerning the second annealing step in N2 atmosphere, films treated at 460 °C showed lower catalytic activity as compared to those treated at 420 °C. Apparently, an increase of the annealing temperature is not beneficial for the final performance. For all investigated CIS electrodes, irradiation with white light triggers a significant increase in the reduction current density (Figure S2).

sections.heading: Gas Chromatography
sections.text: A potentiostatic electrolysis experiment was done in the same solution at a potential of −1.77 V vs NHE for 1 h under ambient light condition. Figure S7 shows the trend of the reduction current during the 1-h potentiostatic reduction. First, the current was a bit increasing and then somehow remained constant for some time and started to decrease. This experiment of course showed that the electrode is not as such stable during the long-term electrolysis. This might be associated with the increased adsorption of tetrabutylammonium cation with time on the active site if it mediates the one-electron carbon dioxide reduction reaction as observed in case pyridine adsorption effect on electrochemically prepared CIS films [41, 52]. After 1-h electrolysis, a gas sample was taken using a headspace from the part of the cell above the solution and analyzed using gas chromatography to identify the formed product. As can be seen in Fig. 6, the product from the analysis of the gas sample is carbon monoxide (CO). No hydrogen gas was detected in the sample. By using one-compartment electrolysis cell, back oxidation of the CO might be a possible reaction although its solubility in acetonitrile is very low.

Usually no or little difference in the amount is observed when the reduction is performed in an H-cell [39]. Similar experiments in the same solvent electrolyte system detect carbonates in the product [40]. The oxidation of the formed carbonate might be another possibility in one-compartment cell. There are no sufficient literature reports about the counter reactions at the anode.
Using the internal calibration curve of the GC, the amount of CO in the headspace sample injected for GC analysis is determined to be 0.55 Vol % of the total amount of the gas taken with the headspace. This value is used to calculate the total ratio in the gas phase volume of the electrochemical cell (30 ml) and to estimate the amount of product (CO) dissolved in the liquid phase (electrolyte) of the electrochemical cell.
Faradaic efficiency was determined according to Eq. 4 [39]:

where nCO gas is the number of COmolecules in the gas phase, nCO sol is the number of CO molecules dissolved in solution, and ne is the number of electrons put into the system during the electrolysis experiment.
The number of mole CO in the gas phase is calculated from the GC analysis, and the number of mole CO dissolved in the electrolyte solution was estimated by using Henry’s Law (Eq. 5) where p is the partial pressure of the solute CO, kH is Henry’s constant, andC is the concentration of CO in solution.
p ¼ kHC ð5Þ
A Henry constant kH of 2507 atm mol −1 solvent per mol CO is applied in the calculations [39, 66]. The numbers of electrons consumed are calculated from the total charge obtained by integrating the electrical current
with respect to time of electrolysis. Based on Eq. 1, the faradaic efficiency for the reduction of CO2 into CO was found to be 20 %±1. Even though the solubility of the main product CO is very low in acetonitrile, its back oxidation on the counter electrode in one-compartment cell might be one of the losses in faradaic efficiency. The other loss might be the dimerization of the CO2 radical anion to form oxalate as a product. The clearly observed loss of course is the unstable nature of the CIS film with time as shown in the electrolysis experiment (Figure S7).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text:
In this study, the preparation of CIS films using layer by layer spin coating of a precursor solution (sol-gel method) and subsequent annealing is described. The XRD analysis showed (112), (204)/(220), and (116)/(312) planes of tetragonal CIS semiconductor (as documented JCPDS cart no. 270159). From the optical absorption spectrum of a CIS film and the extrapolated (αhv)2 value in the (αhv)2-hv plot, an optical band gap of 1.36 eV is calculated. The electrochemical and photoelectrochemical catalytic activity of CIS films on the reduction of carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide is clearly shown. With bare ITO, no significant reduction current was observed, but when it is modified with CIS film, a relatively high reduction current density was observed due to the CIS film catalyzing the electrochemical reduction of CO2 into CO at lower potential with the onset at −0.6 V vs NHE. Interestingly, a photoelectrochemical catalytic effect of CIS was also observed with the increase in reduction current density by illumination of the electrode with white light. The GC analysis confirmed that the main reduction product is carbonmonoxide formed with a faradaic efficiency of 20 (±1)%.
